items.prompt: Given a nested list such as [1, [2, [3, 4]], 5], return the sum of all integers at any depth.
items.why: The structure is defined in terms of itself: sum(list) = numbers + sum of each sub-list. A direct recursion, with nothing to undo or prune.

items.prompt: Count the number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, for n up to 10^4.
items.why: ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2) recomputes the same subproblems exponentially often. Each answer depends on the previous two → Fibonacci-style DP in O(n).

items.prompt: Place n queens on an n×n board so that no two attack each other; return all placements.
items.why: Choose a column per row, abandon a partial board as soon as it conflicts, and undo the choice → backtracking (recursion plus pruning).

items.prompt: Without any loop, print n, n−1, …, 1 and then 1, 2, …, n (e.g. n = 3 → 3 2 1 1 2 3).
items.why: Print once on the way down (before the call) and once on the way back up (after it). Those are the two phases of a recursive call, and there is no matching or scanning signal.

items.prompt: Return all lowercase strings of length n using only the letters 'a', 'b', 'c'.
items.why: Generate all → three calls per position, depth n, 3^n leaves. Nothing repeats and nothing is pruned, so plain tree recursion. DP would only help if you were counting.

items.prompt: Return the values of a binary tree level by level, from top to bottom.
items.why: 'Level by level' is arrival order → a queue (BFS). Recursion naturally goes deep first.

items.prompt: Given a string of balanced brackets, check that every closing bracket matches the most recent unmatched opening one, for strings up to 10^6 characters.
items.why: Matching the most recent opener is LIFO. Use an explicit stack: recursion on 10^6 nested brackets would exceed the recursion limit.

items.prompt: Evaluate an expression given as nested tuples, e.g. ('+', 1, ('*', 2, 3)) → 7, where any operand can itself be such a tuple.
items.why: The input is defined in terms of itself: value(expr) = apply op to value(left) and value(right). Each sub-expression is visited once, so there's nothing to cache or undo.
